In [[graph theory]], a '''bivariegated graph''' is a graph whose vertex set can be [[partition of a set|partitioned]] into two equal parts such that each vertex is adjacent to exactly one vertex from the other set not containing it.<ref name="bedsan">{{harvtxt|Bednarek|Sanders|1973}}.</ref><ref name="bcn">{{harvtxt|Bhat-Nayak|Choudum|Naik|1978}}.</ref><ref name="riddle">{{harvtxt|Riddle|1978}}.</ref>
In a bivarigated graph ''G'' with 2''n'' vertices, there exists a set of ''n'' independent edges such that no odd number of them lie on a cycle of ''G''.

==Examples==
The [[Petersen graph]], shown below, is a bivariegated graph: if one partitions it into an outer pentagon and an inner five-point star, each vertex on one side of the partition has exactly one neighbor on the other side of the partition. More generally, the same is true for any [[generalized Petersen graph]] formed by connecting an outer polygon and an inner star with the same number of points; for instance, this applies to the [[Möbius–Kantor graph]] and the [[Desargues graph]].
[[Image:Petersen1 tiny.svg|center|150px]]
Any [[hypercube graph]], such as the four-dimensional hypercube shown below, is also bivariegated. 
[[Image:Hypercubecentral.svg||center|150px]]
However, the graph shown below is not bivariegated. Whatever you choose the three independent edges, one of them is an edge of a cycle.
[[Image:6n-graf.svg|center|150px]]

==Bivariegated trees==
A tree ''T'' with 2''n'' vertices, is bivariegated if and only if the [[independence number]] of ''T'' is ''n'', or, equivalently, if and only if it has a [[perfect matching]].<ref name="bedsan"/>

==Generalizations==
The '''''k''-varigated graph''', ''k''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;3, can be defined similarly. A graph is said to be ''k''-varigated if its vertex set can be partitioned into ''k'' equal parts such that each vertex is adjacent to exactly one vertex from every other part not containing it.<ref name="bcn"/> 

==Notes==
* Characterizing the [[degree sequence]]s of bivariegated graphs has been an unsolved problem in graph theory.
